circumvent

/sur-kum-VENT/ - the stress falls on VENT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Circumvent means to get around an obstacle — to find a clever route past a rule, barrier, or safeguard instead of meeting it head-on.

To circumvent the new tariff, the importer rerouted its cargo through a port two borders away, where the crates were relabeled and sailed on as domestic goods.

Example

The district's new firewall blocked the gaming sites by name, so within a week the students had circumvented it: someone discovered that the library's own translation tool would fetch any page whole and display it, 'translated' from English into English.

Notice that nobody broke through the firewall or switched it off. Circumventing is the art of the route around — the barrier stays standing, untouched and technically obeyed, while the traffic it was built to stop flows past on a path its designers never imagined.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bypass: To bypass is simply to go around — the highway bypasses the town, and no one calls it clever. Circumvent adds intent and ingenuity: the obstacle is studied, then outmaneuvered, and it is usually an obstacle somebody put there on purpose.

sidestep: To sidestep is to dodge in the moment — a quick step around an awkward question at a press conference. Circumvent is premeditated: a route planned in advance around a rule, a fee, or a safeguard — engineering, where sidestepping is reflex.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

confront: meets the obstacle head-on instead of finding a way around it

comply: follows the rule exactly as written, asking for no way out

Where it sits · how openly the rule is defied

sidestep → circumvent → flout

sidestep vs. circumvent: Sidestep is milder than circumvent: you sidestep an awkward question in the moment, while circumventing takes planning — a whole route engineered around the rule itself.

flout vs. circumvent: Flout goes further than circumvent: to circumvent is to slip around a rule while leaving it standing, but to flout is to break it in the open and dare anyone to object.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — circum-: around (Latin)

Root — vent: come (Latin venire)

Put it together: Latin circum (around) plus venire (to come) builds the picture exactly: to come around. Where a wall cannot be climbed, you arrive on its far side anyway. The same venire walks through convene, intervene, and prevent — English is full of comings, once you know the root to look for.

Use the root in a new word: intervene: The referee let the shoving go for two seconds, then intervened, and the match restarted with tempers cooled.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / strategic

Circumvent is the planner's word — cool, procedural, at home in legal briefs and security bulletins. It passes no verdict by itself: you can circumvent a censor or your own school's firewall, and only context decides which was admirable. Note what it always implies: the rule or barrier is left standing. Repealing a rule removes it; breaching one breaks it; circumventing walks around it and leaves it technically intact. In this unit's company, guile is the trait and a ruse is the trick — circumvent is the route.
